To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients with ST-segments elevation myocardial infarcion with previous coronary artery by-pass grafting had a delay to mechanical percutaneous coronary intervetion and lower rates of patency of the intervened vessel and worse clinical outcomes.

in patients with ST-segement elevation myocardial infarcation and previous coronary artery bypass surgery who underwent primary percutaneous intervention, there was a significant increase in adverse cardiovascular outcomes.

patients with ST-segmenet elevation myocardial infarcion who had previous CABG were more likely to undergo a delay to reperfusion and were less likely to have successful reperfusion of the infarction related artery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of previous CABG on outcomes in patients with ST-segments elevation myocardial infact.
the effects of the antithrobolytic regimen on outcomes of patients with a history of CAB and ST-segment myocardial infarct.

the effect of previous CABG on the clinical and angiographic outcomes and the relation with the different antithrombin regimens in patients undergoing primary percutaneous intervention for ST-segment elevation MI.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the outcomes in this small cohort of patients with ST segment elevation myocardial infraction and a history of CAB were not as good as in patients without CAB and that the outcomes were not influenced by the antithrombin regimen.

the outcomes of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction are worse in patients with a history of previous CABG, and that this is likely due to a delay in the time to reperfusion, and not to the antithrombolytic therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the outcomes of patients with previous CABG were worse, and the reasons for these worse outcomes are likely related to the delay in mechanical reperfusion, lower rates of final revascularization, and higher rates of saphenous graft interventions.

patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarctions who have previously undergone coronary artery bypass graft surgery have a greater risk of adverse outcomes, and this is not affected by the antithrombin regimen used.

previous coronary artery bypass surgery was associated with a significant delay to mechanical revascularization in patients with ST-segement elevation myocardial infarcion, lower rates of periprocedural success, and higher risk for major adverse cardiovascular events at 3 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients with previous CABG should be treated with primary per cutaneous coronary intervention as early as possible.
patients with previous coronary bypass grafting who undergo primary percutaneous intervention for ST elevation myocardial infarcction are at higher risk for adverse clinical outcomes.
patients who had previous coronary artery bypass surgery and present with ST-segment elevated myocardial infarctions are at increased risk for ischemic stroke and target vessel revascularisation.
